text: From NPR News, it's DAY TO DAY.

With the stock market soaring, financial experts say we're headed for yet another round of merger mania. But no one thought the wave would hit quite this quickly. Since the Dow closed at an all-time high on Friday, more than $100 billion in mergers have been announced, including a huge one, today. The British banking giant Barclays will shell out 67 billion euros for its Dutch rival ABN Amro. That's a deal worth more than $91 billion in U.S. dollars.
Marketplace's Sam Eaton joins us now.
Sam, 91 billion. That is quite a chunk of change. What's the significance of this merger?

Alex, this is huge for the banking world. We're talking about the largest bank takeover in history. It's the world's fourth largest merger ever. Together the two banks will have a market value of $190 billion with 47 million global customers.

But the significance really comes down to what's behind those numbers. Analysts say the ABN/Barclays merger is a test case of sorts for even larger bank mergers in Europe, which they say is due for a wave of consolidation. This would come on the heels of the mega-mergers that began in the U.S. several years ago, and as of yet have failed to jump across the pond to Europe.
But this merger isn't a done deal yet, right? What needs to happen before it's actually wrapped up?

Yeah, it's definitely not a done deal. As with most mega-mergers, there's always a little drama. The ABN/Barclays merger still needs to be approved by shareholders. And that leaves some wiggle room for a group of rival bidders, led by Royal Bank of Scotland to try to woo ABN. And this is where the drama lies.

Just hours before the rival banks were scheduled to meet with ABN, ABN announced that as part of the Barclays deal it was going to sell its Chicago-based LaSalle Bank to Bank of America for $21 billion. So the rival bidders then abruptly canceled their meeting this morning with ABN, because for them the LaSalle Bank, with its large presence in the Midwestern United States, was the main attraction.
Bank of America, they're in this. What's in it for them?

Basically, a deal that was too hard for Bank of America to resist. B of A has been trying to build its presence in Chicago, which is the third largest deposit market in the U.S. Its acquisition of LaSalle instantly thrusts it into the number one spot.
I talked to banking consultant Burt Ely, and he said B of A's move is part of a long-term strategy.

Up until now, it's had a relatively minor presence in one of the largest economic centers of the country. And this deal allows it - almost gives it a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to really build a good, solid, broad presence in Chicago and throughout the Midwest.
Now, Chicago's banking sector has so far avoided the presence of competing mega-banks, but now with JP Morgan Chase ousted from its number one spot there, the games begin.
Thanks so much, Sam. Sam Eaton of public radio's daily business show Marketplace. It's produced by American Public Media.
From NPR News, it's DAY TO DAY.

The car business is different today. Toyota reports it sold more cars and trucks during the first three months of this year than any other manufacturer in the world. That moves Toyota one step closer to claiming the number one spot in annual global car sales. That is a place that has belonged to General Motors for 76 years.
MARKETPLACE's Sam Eaton joins us. Sam, analysts have been expecting Toyota to get to the number one spot for some time now, but I guess it's there.

Yeah, and wasn't expected so quickly. The reason you don't have to look further than the price of gasoline right now, Alex, to get a pretty good idea of what's behind that growth - here, you have two car companies that have taken very different paths over the last decade or so. GM, along with the other U.S. automakers Ford and Chrysler have really invested in large trucks and SUVs that Americans couldn't get enough of up until a few years ago. And then you have Toyota, which staked its future on smaller, more reliable and more fuel-efficient cars.

And with rising gas prices, you can guess which strategy is now paying off, and it shows in the numbers. Toyota outsold GM in the first quarter by around 90,000 vehicles. So it's a huge milestone for the Japanese automaker.
Now, do people think in some way, well, this is one quarter, maybe -or is this, yeah - I mean, has - have things really turned?

That - it's inevitable. I mean, most analysts say it's inevitable that Toyota will reach the number one spot. And I think the important thing here is that there are pitfalls to being in that number one spot as well, the most significant being that it makes you a target. Toyota has already been singled out in the U.S. and Europe for trade restrictions, so it's sensitive about being seen as too big or too aggressive.
Uh-huh.

This is a company that's built its reputation on quality and reliability, so you're not likely to see them tooting their own horn about being in the number one spot. So the bottom line is that actually neither of these companies see this as a race.
Well, what about GM?

It's - you know, they're definitely - GM is definitely is playing down the news here. I talked to auto analyst David Healy at Burnham Securities. And he says given the troubles facing the U.S. automakers, GM is more concerned about returning to profitability than any number of cars it sells.

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID HEALY (Automotive Analyst, Burnham Securities)
text: Yes, it's a kind of a psychological blow to become number two. But the key factor is that they're getting back into the black of the United States and on a sustainable basis and, incidentally, growing very rapidly overseas.
Now, of the big three U.S. automakers, GM has definitely been the most successful on the global market, and it's really trying to stress that its future is as an international automaker.
Thank you, Sam. Sam Eaton of Public Radio's daily business show MARKETPLACE, produced by American Public Media.
From NPR News, it's DAY TO DAY.

As we heard earlier in the program, President Bush extended a helping hand today to Americans on the verge of defaulting on their home loans. But do these borrowers truly deserve help? A new study by the Mortgage Bankers Association says not necessarily.
Here to explain is MARKETPLACE's Sam Eaton.
Sam, what exactly did this report find?

Alex, it looks at places or it found that in places like Las Vegas, Arizona and Florida, where a lot of the speculation has taken place, in this places a quarter to a third of the defaults that are now happening are from investor-owned properties. In parts of California, it's about one in five. These houses and condos are owned by everyone from real estate developers all the way down to amateur speculators, trying to make a quick buck flipping homes. Now that the market is slumped, many of these investors have put little or no money down on their loans, can't get rid of their properties. And according to the Mortgage Bankers Association, many are simply walking away from them and letting the banks clean up the mess.
I talked to real estate economist Karl Case at Wellesley, and he says the fact that so many speculators are now defaulting on their loans shouldn't come as a surprise.

I was in Florida a few years ago and I was picking up a car at a rent-a-car counter and the clerk said to me, what are you doing down here? So I'm giving a talk. And he says, on what? I said real estate. He said, oh, I'm in real estate. I said, really? What do you do? He said I own 21 condominiums. And that made me worry.

Right. And then there's the entire program on A&E called "Flip This House," which is all about flipping properties. So I mean are all these speculators, like the guy in Florida, to blame for what's going on now with the mortgage industry?

Alex, you know, there is slight irony in the fact that this report, which basically is kind of shedding the blame of real estate speculators for the record number of defaults right now, is coming from the trade group that represents the mortgage industry, which of course issued those loans. But the bottom line here is that there's plenty of blame to go around, especially now that home prices are no longer making those double-digit gains.

There weren't many people calling for tighter lending standards back during the boom. A real estate expert that I talk to said the problem was really - it's really the market. With more than a decade of gains and housing, people and lenders begin to think that there was no end in sight, and now of course that's proven to be wrong.
Let's talk about this aide package announced today. Who actually does deserve help at this point?

It's - you know, this is a really good question. And you can distinguish the kinds of loans made to people who live in their homes from those made to investors. So it is possible to single out those who, some would say, are the most deserving of the government's help. But economically, I think that distinction matters less. From the economy standpoint, foreclosures are foreclosures and the market is going to react accordingly. And the more people default on their loans, the more everyone takes a hit as home prices fall.
Thanks so much, Sam.
That's Sam Eaton of public radio's daily business show MARKETPLACE. It's produced by American Public Media.
